title: Why a bend is worth money

cues.text: Here is the tangent again, and here it is walking along the curve. Watch the tangent itself, not the point.
It is turning. The gradient is not a fixed number: it has a gradient of its own.
the second gradient. How fast the steepness itself is changing.
One dash for the steepness. Two dashes for how fast the steepness is changing. That is all the second one means.
Two futures, equally likely. One bad, one good, the same distance either side of where we are now.
Join them. The middle of that line is the average of the two values — what you get on average if the future goes one way or the other.
And it is higher than the curve. The average of the two values beats the value at the average. The gap is pure bend — and it is exactly the gap chapter five was about.
So a value that bends upwards is worth more when the future is uncertain than when it is not. That is the whole reason the second gradient appears at all.
A curve that bends the other way loses by the same argument. The chord sits below it, so uncertainty costs rather than pays.
And a straight line — no bend at all — is the one case where uncertainty makes no difference whatsoever. Which is precisely why the textbook, which draws straight lines, never sees any of this.
two dashes: how fast the steepness changes
a bend up puts the average above the curve
so uncertainty adds value to a bent thing
and does nothing at all to a straight one
